title: Urinary tract infection (child)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, paediatric ward
summary: Test urine when symptoms suggest UTI or fever has no source, collecting clean catch urine before antibiotics. Under 3 months: refer and give IV antibiotics. Upper UTI: oral cefalexin for 7 to 10 days (IV if vomiting or very unwell); lower UTI: trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin for 3 days. Image by age and atypical or recurrent features.

sections.title: When to suspect and test
items: Features that make UTI more likely (NICE): dysuria, frequency, new bedwetting, foul-smelling, dark or cloudy urine, visible haematuria, reduced fluid intake, fever, shivering, abdominal, loin or suprapubic pain or tenderness, capillary refill over 3 seconds, previous confirmed UTI.
Features that make it less likely: no dysuria, nappy rash, breathing difficulty, abnormal chest sounds or ear examination, fever with a known alternative cause.

Test urine when these features are present and in any febrile child under 5 with no obvious source; consider it in an unwell child even without them. Do not routinely test children 3 months and over who have an obvious infection elsewhere.
Upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis): bacteriuria with fever 38 °C or more, or bacteriuria with loin pain or tenderness. Bacteriuria without systemic features: lower UTI (cystitis).

Record risk factors for serious pathology: poor urine flow, previous UTI, recurrent unexplained fever, antenatal renal abnormality, family history of VUR or renal disease, constipation, dysfunctional voiding, enlarged bladder or abdominal mass, spinal lesion, poor growth, high blood pressure.

sections.title: Urine collection and testing
items: Collect urine before antibiotics, but never delay treating a seriously ill child. Use clean catch where possible, then urine collection pads; catheter or ultrasound-guided suprapubic aspiration when non-invasive methods fail. Never use cotton wool, gauze or sanitary pads.
If culture cannot start within 4 hours, refrigerate the sample or use boric acid.
Under 3 months: send urgent microscopy and culture; do not rely on dipstick.

3 months to under 3 years (dipstick): leukocyte esterase and nitrite both negative, no antibiotic and no culture unless a culture criterion applies; either positive, send culture and start antibiotics.

3 years and over: both positive, treat (culture if high or intermediate risk or previous UTI); nitrite positive only, treat if the sample is fresh and send culture; leukocyte esterase positive only, culture and treat only with clear clinical UTI; both negative, look for another cause.

Always culture if: suspected pyelonephritis, high or intermediate risk of serious illness, age under 3 months, positive dipstick, recurrent UTI, no response in 24 to 48 hours, or dipstick and clinical picture disagree.

AAP (age 2 to 24 months): diagnose UTI only with pyuria and/or bacteriuria on urinalysis plus at least 50 000 CFU/mL of one uropathogen in a catheter or suprapubic specimen; bag specimens are unreliable for culture.

sections.title: Who needs referral and IV antibiotics
items: Under 3 months with suspected UTI: refer immediately to paediatrics and give IV antibiotics as for fever under 3 months (third-generation cephalosporin plus amoxicillin or ampicillin).
High risk of serious illness or suspected sepsis at any age: refer urgently and manage as sepsis.
Upper UTI over 3 months: consider paediatric referral. Starting oral or parenteral treatment is equally effective (AAP); give IV if vomiting, unable to take oral medicines or severely unwell.

IV options (NICE): ceftriaxone 50 to 80 mg/kg once daily (max 4 g/day), co-amoxiclav 30 mg/kg three times daily (max 1.2 g per dose), cefuroxime, or gentamicin or amikacin once daily with level monitoring. Review IV by 48 hours and step down to oral for 10 days in total.

sections.title: Oral antibiotics (3 months and over)
items: Upper UTI: cefalexin 12.5 mg/kg twice daily (25 mg/kg two to four times daily, max 1 g per dose, if severe) for 7 to 10 days; co-amoxiclav only if culture shows susceptibility (NICE). AAP gives 7 to 14 days in total.

Lower UTI: trimethoprim 4 mg/kg twice daily (max 200 mg per dose) if resistance risk is low, or nitrofurantoin 750 micrograms/kg four times daily, for 3 days. Second choice: nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin or cefalexin guided by culture.
Choose by previous culture results and the local antibiogram. A child on prophylaxis who develops UTI needs a different antibiotic, not a higher dose of the same one.
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, and do not re-test urine after treatment in a child who is well.

sections.title: Imaging after confirmed UTI
items: Atypical UTI: seriously ill, poor urine flow, abdominal or bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, no response to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or non-E. coli organism. Recurrent: 2 or more upper UTIs, 1 upper plus 1 or more lower, or 3 or more lower UTIs.
Under 6 months: ultrasound within 6 weeks if responding well; if atypical or recurrent, ultrasound during the illness plus DMSA at 4 to 6 months and MCUG.

6 months to under 3 years: atypical, ultrasound during the illness and DMSA; recurrent, ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA. MCUG not routine; consider it for dilatation on ultrasound, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or family history of VUR.
3 years and over: atypical, ultrasound during the illness; recurrent, ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA. No MCUG. Scan toilet-trained children with a full bladder and measure post-void volume.

AAP differs: renal and bladder ultrasound after every first febrile UTI at 2 to 24 months; VCUG only if ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, scarring or signs of high-grade VUR or obstruction, or after a recurrent febrile UTI.
If MCUG is done, give 3 days of oral prophylactic antibiotic with the MCUG on the second day.

sections.title: Prevention and follow-up
items: No routine antibiotic prophylaxis after a first UTI. Treat constipation and dysfunctional voiding, encourage enough water, and allow unhurried access to clean toilets.
Tell carers UTI can recur: seek prompt assessment, ideally within 48 hours, for future fevers (AAP).

Refer recurrent UTI or abnormal imaging to paediatrics. With renal scarring, monitor height, weight, blood pressure and proteinuria; bilateral defects, impaired renal function, hypertension or proteinuria need a paediatric nephrologist.
No routine follow-up when imaging is normal or not indicated; give imaging results to families in writing.

sections.title: India and out-of-scope groups
items: India: E. coli resistance to co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins (ESBL) is common. Always send culture, choose empirical therapy from the local antibiogram, and review at 48 hours with the culture result.
Oral cefixime 8 mg/kg once daily (max 400 mg), widely used in India and listed by the AAP, is an option when the organism is susceptible.
NICE NG224 does not cover children with catheters, neurogenic bladder, known uropathy, renal disease, immunosuppression or those in ICU: seek specialist advice.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Culturing bag urine or delaying transport: contamination leads to overdiagnosis and unnecessary imaging.
Using CRP alone to separate upper from lower UTI.
Treating a dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase only, without clinical UTI: the source may be outside the urinary tract.
Using nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis: it is for lower UTI only.
Missing obstruction when fever persists beyond 48 hours on appropriate antibiotics: this is an atypical UTI needing ultrasound during the illness.

drugs.name: Cefalexin
drugs.dose: 12.5 mg/kg orally twice daily for 7 to 10 days (upper UTI) or 3 days (lower UTI); severe: 25 mg/kg two to four times daily (max 1 g per dose)
drugs.notes: NICE first-choice oral agent for pyelonephritis from 3 months.

drugs.name: Co-amoxiclav (oral)
drugs.dose: Amoxicillin component 20 to 40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses (max 500 mg amoxicillin per dose) for 7 to 10 days
drugs.notes: NICE: only if culture shows susceptibility. AAP dose range.

drugs.name: Trimethoprim
drugs.dose: 4 mg/kg orally twice daily (max 200 mg per dose) for 3 days
drugs.notes: Lower UTI when resistance risk is low.

drugs.name: Nitrofurantoin
drugs.dose: 3 months to 11 years: 750 micrograms/kg orally four times daily for 3 days; 12 to 15 years: 50 mg four times daily
drugs.notes: Lower UTI only. Avoid if eGFR below 45 mL/min.

drugs.name: Cefixime
drugs.notes: AAP oral option; common in India. Use culture results.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 50 to 80 mg/kg IV once daily (max 4 g/day)
drugs.notes: IV first choice from 3 months if vomiting or very unwell; step down to oral by 48 hours if possible.

drugs.name: Co-amoxiclav (IV)
drugs.dose: 30 mg/kg IV three times daily (max 1.2 g per dose)
drugs.notes: Only in combination or if culture shows susceptibility (NICE).

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.dose: 7 mg/kg IV once daily initially, then adjust to serum levels
drugs.notes: Check renal function and levels; limit the course (usually no more than 7 days).

drugs.name: Amikacin
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg IV once daily initially, then adjust to serum levels
drugs.notes: Useful where ESBL organisms are common; monitor renal function and levels.
